```meta
severity: high
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened:** `GameEventsClientService.submitMove` wraps its signed `post()` call in a bare `try/catch` that silently swallows any failure, a design choice inherited unchanged from the WS-era `sendMove` ("surfaces as nothing happened, same as the old socket's silent drop-if-not-open behavior"). That catch was written when the only realistic failure was a dropped network call. REQ-ARC-13 changed what can throw inside that same call: `post()`'s SigV4 signing now depends on `cognitoCredentialsProvider`'s newly-added authenticated-role credential resolution/refresh, introduced specifically to satisfy AC#5 (session survival past the access-token lifetime). An auditor's fourth independent run of the exact AC#5 journey (two solo runs, two full batches) reproduced a real failure: the account player's first post-wait move never reached any `GameMoveFunction` CloudWatch log group at all (confirmed by log-group search on the exact `gameId`) -- the click resolved with no visible error, and the game eventually resolved by forfeit. Three of four runs passed clean, so the coder's and tester's own (smaller) verification samples never saw it.

**Why it matters:** a catch-all written to accept one class of failure (an offline/dropped network call, an acceptable UX trade at the time) silently expands its blast radius the moment a call it wraps starts depending on new failure-prone machinery -- here, credential refresh -- without anyone re-examining whether the original "fail silently" justification still holds for the NEW thing that can now throw inside the same block. The failure is real and material (it undermines the exact acceptance criterion the new dependency exists to satisfy) but is invisible to a small number of clean runs, since the underlying race is probabilistic.

**Pattern to encode:** when a change adds a new dependency (especially one with its own async refresh/retry lifecycle, like a credentials provider) inside an existing fire-and-forget catch-all, re-audit whether that catch's original "swallow and move on" justification still applies to every new thing that can now throw inside it -- and if the acceptance criterion the new dependency exists to prove is "survives X," budget more than 1-2 verification runs before trusting a clean pass, since credential-refresh races are exactly the class of failure a small sample under-detects.

## LRN-2026-08-22-d: "Documented in the API description" needs a literal artifact check, not a substitute-document check

```meta

stack: [python, fastapi, openapi]

```

**What happened:** REQ-ARC-3's AC#9 required WebSocket message types to be "documented in the API description." No test asserted on `info.description`'s content, so the gap reached the audit gate undetected.

**Why it matters:** A requirement that names a specific artifact ("the API description," "the OpenAPI document," "the migration file") is testable against that literal artifact, not against whichever document happens to carry the same information in spirit. Substitute documentation can be excellent and still fail the letter of the criterion — and when it does, no test written against the substitute will ever catch it, because the substitute is what the tests were written against too.

**Pattern to encode:** When an acceptance criterion names a specific document/field/endpoint, write (or ask the tester to write) at least one assertion against that literal thing, even when a better, more complete substitute already exists elsewhere. ## LRN-2026-08-22-e: A function parameter honored on only one code path is a latent divergence bug, even when today's caller makes it harmless

```meta

The only production caller always passes that same singleton as `manager`, so the two never diverge today — but the asymmetry was discovered only while writing a direct-dispatch test, and is now something every future test on this function must know and route around.

stack: [angular, amplify-gen2, dynamodb, cognito, lambda-function-url]
req: [REQ-ARC-14]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
severity: HIGH
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened:** REQ-ARC-14's scout contract recommended trusting a body-passed `sub`, "verified" only by confirming the caller held some valid signed credential -- the SAME trust model this codebase's other platform functions already use for their client-asserted `identityId`. An operator ruling overrode this as forgeable: any signed caller (even a guest's own valid credentials) could assert another account's `sub` in the body and permanently steal a resource tied to it. The fix cryptographically verifies the caller's Cognito ID token against the pool's JWKS and acts only on the token's own verified claim. The auditor independently re-attacked the deployed endpoint: forged/tampered/missing tokens all rejected at 401; a forged `sub` riding alongside a real token was structurally unreachable (the handler never parses it); and a real token submitted while a *different* identity's credentials did the IAM signing still resolved to the token's own account, never the signer's -- proving the two trust layers (coarse IAM signing, fine-grained token verification) are genuinely independent and composable, not redundant.

**Why it matters:** most authenticated actions in a system are fine with "some valid signed caller" as the whole trust model -- a guest's own pairing, moves, and presence are self-contained to that one session and cost nothing if merely coarse-grained. The trust model silently stops being sufficient the instant an action's correctness depends on WHICH specific account is calling AND its effect is durable/hard-to-reverse (here: permanent, exclusive ownership). Reusing the codebase's existing, working trust pattern by default is the natural move and was exactly the wrong one here.

**Pattern to encode:** before trusting any client-asserted identity field (a body `sub`, a JWT claim read without signature verification, a session id used as if it were proof), ask: does this action's correctness depend on WHICH identity is calling (not just "some" valid one), and is the effect account-scoped and durable/irreversible? If yes to both, the identity must be cryptographically verified server-side against its own issuer (JWKS/JWT verification, not "the caller holds a valid credential for some other coarser-grained gate"), and the verified claim -- never a request-body field of the same name -- is the only thing the handler may act on.

## LRN-2026-08-24-d: Re-own a pinned regression test to encode a not-yet-implemented target design, not just prose

A later completion pass then built directly against the already-written, unambiguous acceptance tests.

Why it matters: a scope note in a tracking document is advisory and re-interpretable; a failing pin is a mechanical, unambiguous contract the next implementer cannot silently under-deliver against or misread. ## LRN-2026-08-24-g: A git-hash-stamped deploy-freshness check is structurally unsound against a "commit the work after it's deployed" operational convention -- verify content, not the stamp, or redesign the check to tolerate the convention

```meta

project: arcade-web
stack: [ci-cd, deploy-verification, angular, amplify]
req: [REQ-ARC-15, REQ-ARC-16]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
severity: warning
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened:** This project's own operating convention is "commit the crew's work at the gate, audit after" -- meaning a Hosting deploy routinely happens against an uncommitted working tree, and the deploy script's own `data-build-id` stamp substitution captures whatever `git rev-parse --short HEAD` was AT THAT MOMENT (the previous REQ's commit), not the commit that will eventually contain the deployed content. REQ-ARC-15's audit first flagged this as a manual-observation WARNING, content-hash-verified as non-functional. One REQ later, REQ-ARC-16 hit the identical gap, but this time an automated e2e test (`00-deploy-freshness.spec.ts`) added specifically to catch stale bundles now hard-fails on it deterministically, every run, reproduced 2/2 in two independent fresh batches -- a mechanical guard defeating itself against the exact convention it coexists with.

**Why it matters:** A freshness check built on a baked-in stamp assumes deploy-then-commit are atomic or ordered commit-then-deploy. Any project where "commit at gate, deploy during work" is a deliberate risk-mitigation convention (not a mistake) will produce this exact false-positive class on every cycle, and a check that hard-fails on it either gets silently ignored (eroding its own value) or blocks merges on a non-issue.

**Pattern to encode:** When a freshness/staleness guard is built on a stamp that only updates at deploy time, and the project's own workflow allows commits after the deploy with no further code changes, either (a) re-run the stamp substitution as an explicit step of the "commit at gate" convention itself, or (b) have the automated check fall back to a stronger content-hash comparison (of a content-addressed build artifact, e.g. a hashed bundle filename) before concluding staleness, rather than trusting the stamp alone.

## LRN-2026-08-24-j: A DynamoDB `ConditionExpression` comparing ISO-8601 timestamp strings from two different language runtimes is not format-agnostic -- lexicographic comparison, not parsed-datetime comparison

```meta
date: 2026-08-24
project: arcade-web
stack: [dynamodb, python, typescript, eventbridge-scheduler, cross-language]
req: [REQ-ARC-17]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
severity: MEDIUM
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened.** `rematch-offer-expiry`'s fired-handler CAS re-check compares a Python-written `offerExpiresAt` (`datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()`, live-verified format: microsecond precision, `+00:00` offset suffix) against a TypeScript-written `:now` (`new Date().toISOString()`, live-verified format: millisecond precision, `Z` suffix) via a plain DynamoDB `ConditionExpression: 'offerExpiresAt <= :now'`. DynamoDB compares String-type attributes byte-wise, not as parsed datetimes -- unlike application code that does `new Date(x).getTime()` (immune to this class entirely; confirmed the codebase's own `grace-sweep/handler.ts` does exactly that and is safe). Because `'+' (0x2B) < '.' (0x2E)` in ASCII, the two producers' differing suffix characters can make a lexicographic comparison disagree with the true chronological ordering when the compared prefixes are close, and a separate truncation-to-whole-seconds step elsewhere in the same request (scheduling the actual fire time) widens the window this can matter in. No test in either language's suite ever constructed the OTHER language's real timestamp format to compare against.

**Why it matters.** Two producers each individually "just using ISO-8601" is not sufficient when the comparison happens inside a datastore's own native conditional-write mechanism rather than in application code -- there is no `Date` parser standing between the two strings to normalize the format difference away. This class is invisible to any test that only ever constructs fixtures in ONE language's own native format.

**Pattern to encode.** Before trusting a cross-language DynamoDB `ConditionExpression`/`FilterExpression` comparison between two timestamp-shaped String attributes, verify (a) which of the two comparison sides is genuinely written by the OTHER runtime in production (not assumed via a same-format test fixture), and (b) whether the actual live formats byte-compare correctly for every case that matters, especially near a boundary. Prefer normalizing both producers to an identical format (fixed fractional-second digit count, identical UTC suffix) at the point of write, or parse-and-compare in application code instead of relying on the datastore's native string ordering.

## LRN-2026-08-22-a: 100% coverage does not prove a signal-exposed WS message type is actually consumed by the UI

```meta
date: 2026-08-22
project: arcade-web
stack: [angular, vitest, websocket, signals]
req: [REQ-ARC-7]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-22
severity: blocker
```

**What happened.** `GameSocketService` (the coder-spec's mandated single owning service for `/ws/game`) correctly exposed all seven server-to-client message types as readonly signals, including `moveError`. The tester wrote a passing unit test asserting `moveError()` updates when a `move_error` frame arrives. Coverage reported 100% line/branch/function on the service and on every component. But no component ever read `gameSocket.moveError()` -- the handoff contract's documented UI action ("transient rejection cue: shake the cell, toast the message; route non-recoverable codes to an error state") was never built. The auditor found this only by grepping for the signal's call sites outside test files, not from any tool output.

**Why it matters.** Coverage tools measure whether producer-side code executed, not whether a consumer exists downstream. A well-tested, fully-covered signal or observable can be entirely dead from the user's perspective while every quality gate reports green. This is structurally invisible to line/branch coverage because there is no untaken branch -- the producer code runs fine every time.

**Pattern to encode.** When a spec mandates a service expose "every message type as a signal" (fan-out architecture), the audit checklist must separately verify each exposed signal has at least one non-test call site, not just that the producer path is covered. Grep for `<signalName>(` outside `*.spec.ts` as a cheap first pass before trusting coverage numbers on message-routing services.

## LRN-2026-08-22-h: A test-constraint-justified DI escape hatch needs a revert trigger, or it becomes permanent silent-failure debt

```meta
date: 2026-08-22
project: arcade-web
stack: [angular, dependency-injection]
req: [REQ-ARC-7]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-22
severity: warning
```

**What happened.** A coder-spec pattern permitted `inject(Router, { optional: true })` in production code, justified entirely by a pre-existing spec file's `TestBed` not providing `Router`: "the optional form only matters for the untouched spec... flag the spec gap to the tester." The tester then fixed the harness to provide `Router` unconditionally for every test, old and new. Nothing then reverted the production code to an unconditional `inject(Router)`. The optional-injection pattern now sits, unnecessarily, on a security-relevant auth-redirect effect: if the "production always has a router" assumption is ever violated, the failure mode is a silent no-op rather than a loud `NullInjectorError`.

**Why it matters.** Escape-hatch patterns adopted to work around a specific, named test constraint are only ever justified while that constraint holds. Nothing in the pattern's own definition created a trigger to check whether the constraint had since been resolved, so the workaround outlived its reason and became permanent, unexamined defensive code on a path where silent failure is the worst possible outcome.

**Pattern to encode.** When a spec sanctions a DI/test workaround "until the tester adds proper coverage," the handoff that closes the gap should also flag the production code for revert-consideration, not just record the new test coverage. The auditor should re-check the stated justification's continued validity every time, not just confirm the pattern was followed.

## LRN-2026-08-22-i: Exhaustive per-value test coverage belongs at the layer that branches on the value, not the layer that merely passes it through

```meta
date: 2026-08-22

stack: [angular, vitest, websocket]
req: [REQ-ARC-7]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-22
severity: suggestion
```

**What happened.** A prior audit suggested a service-layer WS-message spec should parameterize over all 7 members of a discriminated-union code field, since it only tested 2 directly. A later fix exhaustively covered all 7 at the consumer layer (the component that maps each code to distinct UI text) instead. Re-examining the service's actual routing code showed it performs zero per-code branching -- it stores the whole message object regardless of which of the 7 values arrived. Parameterizing the service spec over all 7 values would have tested nothing the 2-value spec did not already prove; the router doesn't care which value it is.

**Why it matters.** "Only N of M enum values are tested at this layer" is not automatically a gap. Whether it is a gap depends on whether that layer's code varies its behavior by value. Flagging it reflexively, without checking for branching, sends fix effort to the wrong file and can produce redundant tests that inflate a suite without adding assurance.

**Pattern to encode.** Before treating partial per-value coverage as a finding, check whether the flagged code path branches on the value at all. If it's a pure pass-through, the exhaustive check belongs at the nearest layer that actually discriminates.

## LRN-2026-08-21-c: openapi-typescript peer-pins TypeScript 5, Angular 22 ships TypeScript 6

**What happened.** `npm install -D openapi-typescript` on a fresh Angular 22 project failed on peer dependency resolution: `openapi-typescript` declares a peer of `typescript@^5`, but Angular 22's scaffold installs TypeScript 6. Do not reach for `--legacy-peer-deps` or downgrade the project's TypeScript version.

## LRN-2026-08-24-b: A fire-and-forget catch-all swallows a newly-introduced credential-refresh failure mode identically to the old, already-accepted network failure it was designed for

```meta

stack: [aws-amplify, cognito, identity-federation, playwright]
req: [REQ-ARC-13]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
severity: high
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened:** `GameEventsClientService.submitMove` wraps its signed `post()` call in a bare `try/catch` that silently swallows any failure, a design choice inherited unchanged from the WS-era `sendMove` ("surfaces as nothing happened, same as the old socket's silent drop-if-not-open behavior"). That catch was written when the only realistic failure was a dropped network call. REQ-ARC-13 changed what can throw inside that same call: `post()`'s SigV4 signing now depends on `cognitoCredentialsProvider`'s newly-added authenticated-role credential resolution/refresh, introduced specifically to satisfy AC#5 (session survival past the access-token lifetime). An auditor's fourth independent run of the exact AC#5 journey (two solo runs, two full batches) reproduced a real failure: the account player's first post-wait move never reached any `GameMoveFunction` CloudWatch log group at all (confirmed by log-group search on the exact `gameId`) -- the click resolved with no visible error, and the game eventually resolved by forfeit. Three of four runs passed clean, so the coder's and tester's own (smaller) verification samples never saw it.

**Why it matters:** a catch-all written to accept one class of failure (an offline/dropped network call, an acceptable UX trade at the time) silently expands its blast radius the moment a call it wraps starts depending on new failure-prone machinery -- here, credential refresh -- without anyone re-examining whether the original "fail silently" justification still holds for the NEW thing that can now throw inside the same block. The failure is real and material (it undermines the exact acceptance criterion the new dependency exists to satisfy) but is invisible to a small number of clean runs, since the underlying race is probabilistic.

**Pattern to encode:** when a change adds a new dependency (especially one with its own async refresh/retry lifecycle, like a credentials provider) inside an existing fire-and-forget catch-all, re-audit whether that catch's original "swallow and move on" justification still applies to every new thing that can now throw inside it -- and if the acceptance criterion the new dependency exists to prove is "survives X," budget more than 1-2 verification runs before trusting a clean pass, since credential-refresh races are exactly the class of failure a small sample under-detects.

## LRN-2026-08-22-d: "Documented in the API description" needs a literal artifact check, not a substitute-document check

```meta
date: 2026-08-22
project: arcade-api
stack: [python, fastapi, openapi]
req: [REQ-ARC-3]
auditor_run: backend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-22
severity: blocker
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened:** REQ-ARC-3's AC#9 required WebSocket message types to be "documented in the API description." The scout, coder, and tester all treated this as satisfied by `frontend-handoff-contract.md`'s WS table (thorough and accurate) and never touched `FastAPI(description=...)` or any route's `description` field to actually mention `move`/`game_state`/`move_error`. No test asserted on `info.description`'s content, so the gap reached the audit gate undetected.

**Why it matters:** A requirement that names a specific artifact ("the API description," "the OpenAPI document," "the migration file") is testable against that literal artifact, not against whichever document happens to carry the same information in spirit. Substitute documentation can be excellent and still fail the letter of the criterion — and when it does, no test written against the substitute will ever catch it, because the substitute is what the tests were written against too.

**Pattern to encode:** When an acceptance criterion names a specific document/field/endpoint, write (or ask the tester to write) at least one assertion against that literal thing, even when a better, more complete substitute already exists elsewhere. Auditors: when a criterion anchors to an artifact, fetch and inspect that literal artifact directly rather than accepting a cross-referenced substitute as proof.

## LRN-2026-08-22-e: A function parameter honored on only one code path is a latent divergence bug, even when today's caller makes it harmless

```meta
date: 2026-08-22
project: arcade-api
stack: [python, fastapi, websockets]
req: [REQ-ARC-3]
auditor_run: backend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-22
severity: warning
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened:** `routers/ws.py::_handle_move(raw, player_id, manager, session_factory)` takes a `manager` parameter and uses it for the success path (`broadcast_game_state(result, manager)`), but its error path (`_send_move_error`) pushes through the imported module-level `connection_manager` singleton directly, ignoring the parameter entirely. The only production caller always passes that same singleton as `manager`, so the two never diverge today — but the asymmetry was discovered only while writing a direct-dispatch test, and is now something every future test on this function must know and route around.

**Why it matters:** A parameter a function accepts but only partially honors is a contract the signature promises and the body breaks. It costs nothing to notice today because there is exactly one caller and one instance in the process; it becomes a real bug the first time a second instance exists (a scoped test harness, a per-tenant registry, a future multi-worker registry) and nobody remembers which half of the function reads the parameter and which half reads the global.

**Pattern to encode:** When reviewing a handler that both accepts a dependency as a parameter and could reach the same dependency via a module-level singleton, check that every code path uses the same source consistently. Flag (WARNING, not BLOCKER, if no caller currently diverges) a function where only some branches honor an injected parameter — it is a design smell worth fixing before the next REQ extends the same handler, not after a real divergence surfaces as a production bug.

## LRN-2026-08-22-h2: 100%/100% coverage cannot catch a cross-call-site ordering defect

## LRN-2026-08-24-a: A harness that seeds a dependency's state directly instead of calling the real producer is blind until two coincidentally-equal identity sources diverge

```meta

origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened:** `game-events-client.service.spec.ts`'s harness seeded `GuestCredentialsStore.set(identityId, ...)` directly instead of calling `service.connect(identityId)` (the real producer of the class's own `connectedIdentityId` field). This worked, undetected, for three prior REQs because the guest-only code path always set both sources to the identical value in the same call -- no test could have told them apart even in principle. **Pattern to encode:** when a class threads an identity/config value through both a locally-owned field and a shared store it also happens to read elsewhere, seed tests via the real producer method, not by writing directly into the shared store -- and add at least one test where the two sources are seeded with DIFFERENTLY-valued data, asserting which one the real call carries. stack: [angular, amplify-gen2, dynamodb, cognito, lambda-function-url]
```meta
req: [REQ-ARC-14]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
severity: HIGH
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened:** REQ-ARC-14's scout contract recommended trusting a body-passed `sub`, "verified" only by confirming the caller held some valid signed credential -- the SAME trust model this codebase's other platform functions already use for their client-asserted `identityId`. An operator ruling overrode this as forgeable: any signed caller (even a guest's own valid credentials) could assert another account's `sub` in the body and permanently steal a resource tied to it. The auditor independently re-attacked the deployed endpoint: forged/tampered/missing tokens all rejected at 401; a forged `sub` riding alongside a real token was structurally unreachable (the handler never parses it); and a real token submitted while a *different* identity's credentials did the IAM signing still resolved to the token's own account, never the signer's -- proving the two trust layers (coarse IAM signing, fine-grained token verification) are genuinely independent and composable, not redundant.

The trust model silently stops being sufficient the instant an action's correctness depends on WHICH specific account is calling AND its effect is durable/hard-to-reverse (here: permanent, exclusive ownership). Reusing the codebase's existing, working trust pattern by default is the natural move and was exactly the wrong one here.

**Pattern to encode:** before trusting any client-asserted identity field (a body `sub`, a JWT claim read without signature verification, a session id used as if it were proof), ask: does this action's correctness depend on WHICH identity is calling (not just "some" valid one), and is the effect account-scoped and durable/irreversible? If yes to both, the identity must be cryptographically verified server-side against its own issuer (JWKS/JWT verification, not "the caller holds a valid credential for some other coarser-grained gate"), and the verified claim -- never a request-body field of the same name -- is the only thing the handler may act on.

## LRN-2026-08-24-d: Re-own a pinned regression test to encode a not-yet-implemented target design, not just prose

```meta
date: 2026-08-24
project: arcade-web
stack: [angular, testing, process]
req: [REQ-ARC-15]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
severity: MEDIUM
origin: crew-auditor
```

What happened: a REQ-ARC-15 crew-run ruling required a watchdog's "settled" conjunction to gain a third leg (chat confirmation), but the literal implementation broke several pre-existing, boundary-protected regression tests pinning the OLD two-leg behavior. Rather than leaving the gap as a disclosed prose scope-note for the next coder pass to rediscover and re-derive, the tester rewrote those exact pins to the NEW target shape -- deliberately making them fail against current, unmodified production code. A later completion pass then built directly against the already-written, unambiguous acceptance tests.

Why it matters: a scope note in a tracking document is advisory and re-interpretable; a failing pin is a mechanical, unambiguous contract the next implementer cannot silently under-deliver against or misread. It also makes the gap's existence impossible to quietly lose track of -- the suite itself reports incomplete work as failing, not green-with-an-asterisk.

Pattern to encode: when a design ruling conflicts with an existing pinned test, and the constrained role cannot edit tests, escalate to the role that CAN (tester/spec-owner) to rewrite the pin to the target shape -- never leave the conflict as unenforced prose, and never silently work around the pinned behavior to avoid touching it. Verify by construction which sibling pins are unaffected before touching them, to avoid scope creep.

## LRN-2026-08-24-g: A git-hash-stamped deploy-freshness check is structurally unsound against a "commit the work after it's deployed" operational convention -- verify content, not the stamp, or redesign the check to tolerate the convention

```meta
date: 2026-08-24
project: arcade-web
stack: [ci-cd, deploy-verification, angular, amplify]
req: [REQ-ARC-15, REQ-ARC-16]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
severity: warning
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened:** This project's own operating convention is "commit the crew's work at the gate, audit after" -- meaning a Hosting deploy routinely happens against an uncommitted working tree, and the deploy script's own `data-build-id` stamp substitution captures whatever `git rev-parse --short HEAD` was AT THAT MOMENT (the previous REQ's commit), not the commit that will eventually contain the deployed content. REQ-ARC-15's audit first flagged this as a manual-observation WARNING, content-hash-verified as non-functional. One REQ later, REQ-ARC-16 hit the identical gap, but this time an automated e2e test (`00-deploy-freshness.spec.ts`) added specifically to catch stale bundles now hard-fails on it deterministically, every run, reproduced 2/2 in two independent fresh batches -- a mechanical guard defeating itself against the exact convention it coexists with.

**Why it matters:** A freshness check built on a baked-in stamp assumes deploy-then-commit are atomic or ordered commit-then-deploy. Any project where "commit at gate, deploy during work" is a deliberate risk-mitigation convention (not a mistake) will produce this exact false-positive class on every cycle, and a check that hard-fails on it either gets silently ignored (eroding its own value) or blocks merges on a non-issue.

**Pattern to encode:** When a freshness/staleness guard is built on a stamp that only updates at deploy time, and the project's own workflow allows commits after the deploy with no further code changes, either (a) re-run the stamp substitution as an explicit step of the "commit at gate" convention itself, or (b) have the automated check fall back to a stronger content-hash comparison (of a content-addressed build artifact, e.g. a hashed bundle filename) before concluding staleness, rather than trusting the stamp alone.

## LRN-2026-08-24-j: A DynamoDB `ConditionExpression` comparing ISO-8601 timestamp strings from two different language runtimes is not format-agnostic -- lexicographic comparison, not parsed-datetime comparison

```meta
date: 2026-08-24
project: arcade-web
stack: [dynamodb, python, typescript, eventbridge-scheduler, cross-language]
req: [REQ-ARC-17]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
severity: MEDIUM
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened.** `rematch-offer-expiry`'s fired-handler CAS re-check compares a Python-written `offerExpiresAt` (`datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()`, live-verified format: microsecond precision, `+00:00` offset suffix) against a TypeScript-written `:now` (`new Date().toISOString()`, live-verified format: millisecond precision, `Z` suffix) via a plain DynamoDB `ConditionExpression: 'offerExpiresAt <= :now'`. DynamoDB compares String-type attributes byte-wise, not as parsed datetimes -- unlike application code that does `new Date(x).getTime()` (immune to this class entirely; confirmed the codebase's own `grace-sweep/handler.ts` does exactly that and is safe). Because `'+' (0x2B) < '.' (0x2E)` in ASCII, the two producers' differing suffix characters can make a lexicographic comparison disagree with the true chronological ordering when the compared prefixes are close, and a separate truncation-to-whole-seconds step elsewhere in the same request (scheduling the actual fire time) widens the window this can matter in. No test in either language's suite ever constructed the OTHER language's real timestamp format to compare against.

**Why it matters.** Two producers each individually "just using ISO-8601" is not sufficient when the comparison happens inside a datastore's own native conditional-write mechanism rather than in application code -- there is no `Date` parser standing between the two strings to normalize the format difference away. This class is invisible to any test that only ever constructs fixtures in ONE language's own native format.

**Pattern to encode.** Before trusting a cross-language DynamoDB `ConditionExpression`/`FilterExpression` comparison between two timestamp-shaped String attributes, verify (a) which of the two comparison sides is genuinely written by the OTHER runtime in production (not assumed via a same-format test fixture), and (b) whether the actual live formats byte-compare correctly for every case that matters, especially near a boundary. Prefer normalizing both producers to an identical format (fixed fractional-second digit count, identical UTC suffix) at the point of write, or parse-and-compare in application code instead of relying on the datastore's native string ordering.

## LRN-2026-08-22-a: 100% coverage does not prove a signal-exposed WS message type is actually consumed by the UI

```meta
date: 2026-08-22
project: arcade-web
stack: [angular, vitest, websocket, signals]
req: [REQ-ARC-7]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-22
severity: blocker
```

**What happened.** `GameSocketService` (the coder-spec's mandated single owning service for `/ws/game`) correctly exposed all seven server-to-client message types as readonly signals, including `moveError`. The tester wrote a passing unit test asserting `moveError()` updates when a `move_error` frame arrives. Coverage reported 100% line/branch/function on the service and on every component. But no component ever read `gameSocket.moveError()` -- the handoff contract's documented UI action ("transient rejection cue: shake the cell, toast the message; route non-recoverable codes to an error state") was never built. The auditor found this only by grepping for the signal's call sites outside test files, not from any tool output.

**Why it matters.** Coverage tools measure whether producer-side code executed, not whether a consumer exists downstream. A well-tested, fully-covered signal or observable can be entirely dead from the user's perspective while every quality gate reports green. This is structurally invisible to line/branch coverage because there is no untaken branch -- the producer code runs fine every time.

**Pattern to encode.** When a spec mandates a service expose "every message type as a signal" (fan-out architecture), the audit checklist must separately verify each exposed signal has at least one non-test call site, not just that the producer path is covered. ## LRN-2026-08-22-h: A test-constraint-justified DI escape hatch needs a revert trigger, or it becomes permanent silent-failure debt

```meta
date: 2026-08-22
project: arcade-web
stack: [angular, dependency-injection]
req: [REQ-ARC-7]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-22
severity: warning
```

**What happened.** A coder-spec pattern permitted `inject(Router, { optional: true })` in production code, justified entirely by a pre-existing spec file's `TestBed` not providing `Router`: "the optional form only matters for the untouched spec... flag the spec gap to the tester." The tester then fixed the harness to provide `Router` unconditionally for every test, old and new. Nothing then reverted the production code to an unconditional `inject(Router)`. The optional-injection pattern now sits, unnecessarily, on a security-relevant auth-redirect effect: if the "production always has a router" assumption is ever violated, the failure mode is a silent no-op rather than a loud `NullInjectorError`.

**Why it matters.** Escape-hatch patterns adopted to work around a specific, named test constraint are only ever justified while that constraint holds. Nothing in the pattern's own definition created a trigger to check whether the constraint had since been resolved, so the workaround outlived its reason and became permanent, unexamined defensive code on a path where silent failure is the worst possible outcome.

**Pattern to encode.** When a spec sanctions a DI/test workaround "until the tester adds proper coverage," the handoff that closes the gap should also flag the production code for revert-consideration, not just record the new test coverage. The auditor should re-check the stated justification's continued validity every time, not just confirm the pattern was followed.

## LRN-2026-08-22-i: Exhaustive per-value test coverage belongs at the layer that branches on the value, not the layer that merely passes it through

```meta

req: [REQ-ARC-7]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-22
severity: suggestion
```

**What happened.** A prior audit suggested a service-layer WS-message spec should parameterize over all 7 members of a discriminated-union code field, since it only tested 2 directly. A later fix exhaustively covered all 7 at the consumer layer (the component that maps each code to distinct UI text) instead. Re-examining the service's actual routing code showed it performs zero per-code branching -- it stores the whole message object regardless of which of the 7 values arrived. Flagging it reflexively, without checking for branching, sends fix effort to the wrong file and can produce redundant tests that inflate a suite without adding assurance.

**Pattern to encode.** Before treating partial per-value coverage as a finding, check whether the flagged code path branches on the value at all. If it's a pure pass-through, the exhaustive check belongs at the nearest layer that actually discriminates.

## LRN-2026-08-21-c: openapi-typescript peer-pins TypeScript 5, Angular 22 ships TypeScript 6

```meta
date: 2026-08-21
project: _seed
stack: [angular, openapi-generator]
req: []
auditor_run: seed@angular
severity: warning
seed: true
```

**What happened.** `npm install -D openapi-typescript` on a fresh Angular 22 project failed on peer dependency resolution: `openapi-typescript` declares a peer of `typescript@^5`, but Angular 22's scaffold installs TypeScript 6. The reflex fixes both make things worse: `--legacy-peer-deps` silently accepts a peer mismatch that may bite later, and downgrading the project's TypeScript to 5.x fights the framework's own pin.

**Why it matters.** The failure looks like a broken package rather than a lagging peer range, so the obvious fixes attack the wrong layer. Downgrading TypeScript project-wide to satisfy one dev-only codegen tool is a worse trade than isolating the tool.

**Pattern to encode.** Run `openapi-typescript` through a version-pinned `npx` invocation (e.g. `npx -y openapi-typescript@latest ...` in its own step) so its peer resolution stays local to that invocation, or add a `resolutions`/`overrides` entry scoped to that package only. Do not reach for `--legacy-peer-deps` or downgrade the project's TypeScript version.

## LRN-2026-08-21-c2: openapi-typescript still pins peer typescript ^5.x, so Angular 22 rejects it

```meta

stack: [angular, typescript, openapi]
req: []

severity: major
origin: human
```

## LRN-2026-08-24-b: A fire-and-forget catch-all swallows a newly-introduced credential-refresh failure mode identically to the old, already-accepted network failure it was designed for

```meta
date: 2026-08-24
project: arcade-web
stack: [aws-amplify, cognito, identity-federation, playwright]
req: [REQ-ARC-13]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
severity: high
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened:** `GameEventsClientService.submitMove` wraps its signed `post()` call in a bare `try/catch` that silently swallows any failure, a design choice inherited unchanged from the WS-era `sendMove` ("surfaces as nothing happened, same as the old socket's silent drop-if-not-open behavior"). That catch was written when the only realistic failure was a dropped network call. REQ-ARC-13 changed what can throw inside that same call: `post()`'s SigV4 signing now depends on `cognitoCredentialsProvider`'s newly-added authenticated-role credential resolution/refresh, introduced specifically to satisfy AC#5 (session survival past the access-token lifetime). An auditor's fourth independent run of the exact AC#5 journey (two solo runs, two full batches) reproduced a real failure: the account player's first post-wait move never reached any `GameMoveFunction` CloudWatch log group at all (confirmed by log-group search on the exact `gameId`) -- the click resolved with no visible error, and the game eventually resolved by forfeit. Three of four runs passed clean, so the coder's and tester's own (smaller) verification samples never saw it.

**Why it matters:** a catch-all written to accept one class of failure (an offline/dropped network call, an acceptable UX trade at the time) silently expands its blast radius the moment a call it wraps starts depending on new failure-prone machinery -- here, credential refresh -- without anyone re-examining whether the original "fail silently" justification still holds for the NEW thing that can now throw inside the same block. The failure is real and material (it undermines the exact acceptance criterion the new dependency exists to satisfy) but is invisible to a small number of clean runs, since the underlying race is probabilistic.

**Pattern to encode:** when a change adds a new dependency (especially one with its own async refresh/retry lifecycle, like a credentials provider) inside an existing fire-and-forget catch-all, re-audit whether that catch's original "swallow and move on" justification still applies to every new thing that can now throw inside it -- and if the acceptance criterion the new dependency exists to prove is "survives X," budget more than 1-2 verification runs before trusting a clean pass, since credential-refresh races are exactly the class of failure a small sample under-detects.

```meta
date: 2026-08-24
project: arcade-web
stack: [angular, amplify-gen2, dynamodb, cognito, lambda-function-url]
req: [REQ-ARC-14]
auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
severity: HIGH
origin: crew-auditor
```

**What happened:** REQ-ARC-14's scout contract recommended trusting a body-passed `sub`, "verified" only by confirming the caller held some valid signed credential -- the SAME trust model this codebase's other platform functions already use for their client-asserted `identityId`. An operator ruling overrode this as forgeable: any signed caller (even a guest's own valid credentials) could assert another account's `sub` in the body and permanently steal a resource tied to it. The fix cryptographically verifies the caller's Cognito ID token against the pool's JWKS and acts only on the token's own verified claim. The auditor independently re-attacked the deployed endpoint: forged/tampered/missing tokens all rejected at 401; a forged `sub` riding alongside a real token was structurally unreachable (the handler never parses it); and a real token submitted while a *different* identity's credentials did the IAM signing still resolved to the token's own account, never the signer's -- proving the two trust layers (coarse IAM signing, fine-grained token verification) are genuinely independent and composable, not redundant.

2	# Graded by crew-evaluator: 0 HIGH, 3 MEDIUM. Entries below are verbatim.
3	
4	## LRN-2026-08-24-c: A client-asserted identity is a claim, not a proof -- cryptographic verification is required the moment an action is account-scoped and irreversible
5	
6	```meta
7	date: 2026-08-24
8	project: arcade-web
9	stack: [angular, amplify-gen2, dynamodb, cognito, lambda-function-url]
10	req: [REQ-ARC-14]
11	auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
12	severity: HIGH
13	origin: crew-auditor
14	```
15	
16	**What happened:** REQ-ARC-14's scout contract recommended trusting a body-passed `sub`, "verified" only by confirming the caller held some valid signed credential -- the SAME trust model this codebase's other platform functions already use for their client-asserted `identityId`. An operator ruling overrode this as forgeable: any signed caller (even a guest's own valid credentials) could assert another account's `sub` in the body and permanently steal a resource tied to it. The fix cryptographically verifies the caller's Cognito ID token against the pool's JWKS and acts only on the token's own verified claim. The auditor independently re-attacked the deployed endpoint: forged/tampered/missing tokens all rejected at 401; a forged `sub` riding alongside a real token was structurally unreachable (the handler never parses it); and a real token submitted while a *different* identity's credentials did the IAM signing still resolved to the token's own account, never the signer's -- proving the two trust layers (coarse IAM signing, fine-grained token verification) are genuinely independent and composable, not redundant.
17	
18	**Why it matters:** most authenticated actions in a system are fine with "some valid signed caller" as the whole trust model -- a guest's own pairing, moves, and presence are self-contained to that one session and cost nothing if merely coarse-grained. The trust model silently stops being sufficient the instant an action's correctness depends on WHICH specific account is calling AND its effect is durable/hard-to-reverse (here: permanent, exclusive ownership). Reusing the codebase's existing, working trust pattern by default is the natural move and was exactly the wrong one here.
19	
20	**Pattern to encode:** before trusting any client-asserted identity field (a body `sub`, a JWT claim read without signature verification, a session id used as if it were proof), ask: does this action's correctness depend on WHICH identity is calling (not just "some" valid one), and is the effect account-scoped and durable/irreversible? If yes to both, the identity must be cryptographically verified server-side against its own issuer (JWKS/JWT verification, not "the caller holds a valid credential for some other coarser-grained gate"), and the verified claim -- never a request-body field of the same name -- is the only thing the handler may act on.
21	
22	## LRN-2026-08-22-a: 100% coverage does not prove a signal-exposed WS message type is actually consumed by the UI
23	
24	```meta
25	date: 2026-08-22
26	project: arcade-web
27	stack: [angular, vitest, websocket, signals]
28	req: [REQ-ARC-7]
29	auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-22
30	severity: blocker
31	```

33	**What happened.** `GameSocketService` (the coder-spec's mandated single owning service for `/ws/game`) correctly exposed all seven server-to-client message types as readonly signals, including `moveError`. But no component ever read `gameSocket.moveError()` -- the handoff contract's documented UI action ("transient rejection cue: shake the cell, toast the message; route non-recoverable codes to an error state") was never built. The auditor found this only by grepping for the signal's call sites outside test files, not from any tool output.
34	
35	**Why it matters.** Coverage tools measure whether producer-side code executed, not whether a consumer exists downstream. A well-tested, fully-covered signal or observable can be entirely dead from the user's perspective while every quality gate reports green. This is structurally invisible to line/branch coverage because there is no untaken branch -- the producer code runs fine every time.
36	
37	**Pattern to encode.** When a spec mandates a service expose "every message type as a signal" (fan-out architecture), the audit checklist must separately verify each exposed signal has at least one non-test call site, not just that the producer path is covered. Grep for `<signalName>(` outside `*.spec.ts` as a cheap first pass before trusting coverage numbers on message-routing services.
38

44	stack: [angular, vitest, websocket]
45	req: [REQ-ARC-7]

A later fix exhaustively covered all 7 at the consumer layer (the component that maps each code to distinct UI text) instead. 51	
52	**Why it matters.** "Only N of M enum values are tested at this layer" is not automatically a gap. Whether it is a gap depends on whether that layer's code varies its behavior by value. Flagging it reflexively, without checking for branching, sends fix effort to the wrong file and can produce redundant tests that inflate a suite without adding assurance.
53	
54	**Pattern to encode.** Before treating partial per-value coverage as a finding, check whether the flagged code path branches on the value at all. If it's a pure pass-through, the exhaustive check belongs at the nearest layer that actually discriminates.

50	| Backend definition | `amplify/backend.ts` |
51	| Auth | `amplify/auth/resource.ts` |
52	| API contract (GraphQL schema) | `amplify/data/resource.ts` |
53	| Lambda functions | `amplify/functions/<name>/` (`resource.ts` + `handler.ts`) |
54	| Generated backend outputs | `amplify_outputs.json` (DO NOT EDIT, not committed) |
55	| End-to-end and visual tests | `e2e/` |
56	
57	`base_package` does not apply. One feature per folder.
58	
59	---
60	
61	## Architecture Patterns
62	
63	### Standalone components only
64	No `NgModule`. New code uses `standalone: true` (the default in Angular 21+). Components, directives, and pipes import their own dependencies via the `imports` array.
65	
66	### Signals for reactive state
67	- Component state: `signal()`, `computed()`, `linkedSignal()`.
68	- Async: `resource()` / `httpResource()` (Angular 20+). Falls back to `toSignal(observable$)` when interop with RxJS is required.
69	- Forms: signal-based forms (`Control` from `@angular/forms/signals`) for new code; existing reactive forms (`FormGroup`) are tolerated but new feature work uses signals.
70	- Do NOT use `BehaviorSubject` for component-local state. Use `signal()`.
71	
72	### OnPush change detection
73	Every new component declares `changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`. The default `Default` strategy is forbidden in new code; it costs performance and hides re-render bugs.
74	
75	### Dependency injection
76	- `inject()` function inside the constructor body or as a class field. Constructor parameter injection is the older style; new code uses `inject()`.
77	- `providedIn: 'root'` for app-wide services. Feature-scoped services use a feature-local provider.
78	
79	### Routing
80	Lazy-load every feature route via `loadComponent` / `loadChildren`. Eager imports are reserved for the shell.
81	
82	---
83	
84	## API Consumption (Amplify Data)
85	
86	The API contract is the Amplify Data schema in `amplify/data/resource.ts`. Agents cite contract items by operation or type name in that schema.
87	
88	1. Front-end code calls the backend only through `generateClient<Schema>()` from `aws-amplify/data`, using the `Schema` type exported by `amplify/data/resource.ts`. Never hand-write GraphQL operation strings, HTTP calls, or copies of schema types.
89	2. Every state change the REQs require the server to decide (moves, matchmaking, ratings, chat moderation, claims) is a custom mutation with a Lambda handler; clients never write game state directly.
90	3. Live updates use schema subscriptions. Correctness never depends on one subscription message arriving (REQ-ARC-4 AC2): clients re-read authoritative state on gaps.
91	4. Never edit `amplify_outputs.json`; `ampx sandbox` generates it.
92	
93	The pinned client version lives in `wopr.yml` (`api_contract.pinned_generator_version`) and must match `package.json`. If a needed operation is missing from the schema, the coder adds it in the same REQ.
94	
95	---
96	
97	## Styling
98	
99	- Component-scoped SCSS unless the project explicitly uses Tailwind.
100	- Theme tokens are CSS custom properties in `src/styles.scss`; components reference tokens, never raw color values.
101	- Global CSS is forbidden except for resets in the shell.
102	
103	---
104	
105	## Anti-Patterns (auditor surfaces these as BLOCKERs)
106	
107	- `@Component` without `changeDetection: OnPush` in new code.
108	- `NgModule` usage in new code.
109	- Hand-written GraphQL operation strings, HTTP calls, or schema type copies instead of `generateClient<Schema>()`.
110	- Hand-edits to `amplify_outputs.json`.
111	- Client code that writes game state the server must decide.
112	- Process or history comments in product source: REQ numbers, audit findings, rulings, learning IDs, dates, or narratives of how the code came to be. Comments explain only non-obvious code.
113	- Reactive forms (`FormGroup`/`FormControl`) for new feature work when signal-based forms are available.
114	- `subscribe()` inside a component body without a teardown. Prefer `async` pipe, `toSignal`, or `takeUntilDestroyed`.
115	- Importing `rxjs/internal/*`. Use the public RxJS surface only.
116	- Accessing `document` / `window` directly. Use `DOCUMENT` token / `WINDOW` token.
117	
118	---
119	
120	## Coverage Gate
121	
122	The five-condition gate (the orchestrator owns and enforces it; the tester records `coverage_status`; the auditor independently re-verifies):
123	
124	1. Build passes. `ng build` exits 0.
125	2. Full test suite passes. `ng test` exits 0.
126	3. Traceability: every acceptance criterion of the REQ maps to at least one named test. Line and branch coverage are recorded as a diagnostic, not a pass metric.
127	4. Single project, no handoff contract. If the REQ changed the schema, the backend typecheck passes and the sandbox deploys.
128	5. Static analysis: `ng lint` and the backend typecheck are clean.
129	
130	---
131	
132	## Spec Maintenance
133	
134	When `spec_writes` is ON (`wopr.yml` `specs.spec_writes`; default OFF), the coder amends this spec when a new pattern emerges. Examples that belong here the moment they are used:
135	
136	- A new component pattern this project will repeat (a route guard idiom, a form composition shape, etc.).
137	- A naming convention for a new category of file.
138	- A decision about how to handle a specific Angular API quirk.
139	- A build-config rule the next coder needs (build-target tweak, dependency version pin, profile gotcha).
140	
141	Two inconsistent patterns are NEVER tolerated. If the new pattern replaces an old one, rewrite the old usage.
142

1	# Tester Spec - WOPR Arcade
2	
3	> **Stack:** Angular 22, Vitest (NOT Jest), Playwright; Amplify Gen 2 backend with TypeScript Lambda functions. Run every node/npm/npx command through `mise exec --`.
4	> **This file:** stack-pre-filled starting point.
5	> **For the deep version:** the generic `tester-spec.template.md` in the crew pack's templates (fetch via `get_pack_template`, `pack="crew"`, `name="tester-spec.template.md"`).
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Requirements Sources
10	
11	| Document | Path | Purpose |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| Implementation tracking | `implementation-tracking.md` | Which REQs need coverage |
14	| Requirements | `requirements/REQ-ARC-<n>.md` | Acceptance criteria per REQ |
15	| Design standard | `requirements/design-standard.md` | Appearance rules (designer-owned `@visual` tests) |
16	| Coder spec | `specs/coder-spec.md` | Commands and production-code rules |
17	| API contract | `amplify/data/resource.ts` | Operation shapes; tests use its `Schema` type |
18	
19	---
20	
21	## Build and Test Commands
22	
23	Use the commands table in `specs/coder-spec.md`. Coverage: `ng test --coverage`. Never point Vitest at individual files.
24	
25	---
26	
27	## Test File Layout
28	
29	| Type | Location | Naming |
30	|---|---|---|
31	| Component test | next to the component | `<name>.component.spec.ts` |
32	| Service test | next to the service | `<name>.service.spec.ts` |
33	| Pipe / directive | next to the source | `<name>.pipe.spec.ts` / `<name>.directive.spec.ts` |
34	| Route guard | next to the guard | `<name>.guard.spec.ts` |
35	| Lambda handler | next to the handler in `amplify/functions/<name>/` | `handler.spec.ts` |
36	| E2E (Playwright) | `e2e/` | `<feature>.e2e-spec.ts` |
37	
38	Co-location is mandatory. Tests do NOT live in a separate `tests/` tree.
39	
40	---
41	
42	## Vitest Configuration
43	
44	- Specs import from `'vitest'` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`, `vi`). Never `'@jest/globals'` or implicit Jest globals.
45	- Spec files end in `.spec.ts`. Never `.test.ts`.
46	- `vi.fn()` for mocks. Never `jest.fn()`.
47	- Async assertions use `await expect(...).resolves` / `await expect(...).rejects`.
48	
49	---
50	
51	## What to Test
52	
53	Every public service method:
54	- Happy path
55	- Null / empty / undefined input
56	- Validation failure / error response
57	
58	Every component:
59	- Renders without throwing
60	- Reacts to input signal changes
61	- Emits expected outputs on user interactions
62	- Handles loading and error states from resources
63	
64	Every route guard:
65	- Allow path
66	- Deny path
67	- Edge cases (no token, expired token, etc. per project rules)
68	
69	Every schema operation (query, mutation, subscription):
70	- Success path
71	- Authorization denied (wrong player, non-participant)
72	- Business rejection (the REQ's named refusal, with its reason)
73	
74	Every acceptance criterion involving two players, timing, or disconnects has an end-to-end test against the deployed sandbox.
75	
76	---
77	
78	## Fixtures and Mocks
79	
80	### Use generated types
81	Test fixtures use the `Schema` type exported by `amplify/data/resource.ts`.
82	Never declare shape-only copies of API models in test files. When the spec changes, the compiler should tell you.
83	
84	### Coverage exclusions
85	Generated files (`amplify_outputs.json`, `.amplify/**`) MUST be excluded from coverage denominators. The exclusion pattern lives in the project's `vitest.config.ts` `coverage.exclude` list. If the coverage math looks wrong on a regenerated client, check this list first.
86	
87	---
88	
89	## Anti-Patterns (auditor surfaces these as BLOCKERs)
90	
91	- `.test.ts` filenames (Vitest convention is `.spec.ts`; mixed conventions break the test runner's discovery).
92	- Imports from `'@jest/globals'` (this is Vitest, not Jest).
93	- Hand-written shape-only copies of schema types in test files.
94	- Unit tests that touch real network; mock at the `generateClient` boundary. End-to-end tests run against the deployed sandbox.
95	- Tests that restate the implementation instead of checking the acceptance criterion.
96	- Tests that depend on render order, animation timing, or `setTimeout` without `vi.useFakeTimers()`.
97	- Snapshot tests for component output. Snapshot rot is real; prefer explicit assertions.
98	- Skipping flaky tests with `it.skip`. Fix the flake or delete the test; never both leave it and ignore it.
99	
100	---
101	
102	## Coverage Gate (tester records, auditor cross-checks)
103	
104	After tests pass, record on the REQ's implementation-tracking log entry:
105	
106	```
107	coverage_status: line XX% / branch YY% / static_analysis: PASS / gate: PASS
108	```
109	
110	Or, when the gate fails:
111	
112	```
113	coverage_status: line XX% / branch YY% / static_analysis: PASS / gate: FAIL (specific reason, e.g. "REQ-CASE-3 missing 404 path")
114	```
115	
116	PASS means:
117	- Build passes.
118	- Full test suite passes (zero new failures).
119	- Every acceptance criterion maps to at least one named test (criterion -> test map on the log entry). Coverage percentages are a diagnostic only.
120	- `ng lint` and the backend typecheck are clean.
121	
122	Never report `gate: PASS` without a fresh `ng test --coverage` measurement. The auditor re-measures and drift is a BLOCKER.
123	
124	---
125	
126	## Spec Maintenance
127	
128	When `spec_writes` is ON (`wopr.yml` `specs.spec_writes`; default OFF), amend this spec when a new coverage shape or fixture idiom emerges. Examples:
129	
130	- A new fixture-construction idiom (builder for nested signal-based forms).
131	- A coverage rule for a new test category.
132	- A new isolation rule discovered after a flaky test was diagnosed.
133	- A naming convention for a new test category (parameterized cases, property-based tests).
134	- A coverage-tool exclusion pattern other test authors will need.
135	
136	---
137	
138	## Visual Regression (only when `wopr.yml` declares `specs.design_spec`)
139	
140	The `crew-designer` role owns these tests; the tester never writes or edits `@visual` tests, and the designer never writes anything else. Listed here because they live in the same e2e tree and the auditor runs them at the gate.
141	
142	- Mechanism: Playwright screenshot assertions (`await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(...)`), one per appearance acceptance criterion, tagged `@visual`.
143	- Command: `specs.visual_check` from `wopr.yml` (canonically `npx playwright test --grep @visual`).
144	- Baselines: committed to the repo at Playwright's default `__screenshots__/` layout. **Only the operator commits or updates a baseline.** The designer generates candidates and lists them; a machine-approved baseline grades the screenshot against itself.

9	## Requirement
10	The server is the sole authority on the board. It decides every move's legality and every outcome; a client can never make an illegal move stick or fabricate a result.
11	
12	## Acceptance criteria
13	1. Only the player whose turn it is may move, and only to an empty cell in the 3x3 grid; any other attempt is rejected with a specific reason and leaves the board unchanged.
14	2. A player who is not a participant of a game cannot affect it.
15	3. A win is detected on any of the 8 lines (3 rows, 3 columns, 2 diagonals) and names the winner and the winning line; a full board with no line is a draw.
16	4. A finished game is immutable: no further move changes it.
17	5. The authoritative game state (board, whose turn, participants, result) can be read at any time and is the source of truth over any live notification.

1	## LRN-2026-08-21-c: openapi-typescript peer-pins TypeScript 5, Angular 22 ships TypeScript 6
2	
3	```meta
4	date: 2026-08-21
5	project: _seed
6	stack: [angular, openapi-generator]
7	req: []
8	auditor_run: seed@angular
9	severity: warning
10	seed: true
11	```
12	
13	**What happened.** `npm install -D openapi-typescript` on a fresh Angular 22 project failed on peer dependency resolution: `openapi-typescript` declares a peer of `typescript@^5`, but Angular 22's scaffold installs TypeScript 6. The reflex fixes both make things worse: `--legacy-peer-deps` silently accepts a peer mismatch that may bite later, and downgrading the project's TypeScript to 5.x fights the framework's own pin.
14	
15	**Why it matters.** The failure looks like a broken package rather than a lagging peer range, so the obvious fixes attack the wrong layer. Downgrading TypeScript project-wide to satisfy one dev-only codegen tool is a worse trade than isolating the tool.
16	
17	**Pattern to encode.** Run `openapi-typescript` through a version-pinned `npx` invocation (e.g. `npx -y openapi-typescript@latest ...` in its own step) so its peer resolution stays local to that invocation, or add a `resolutions`/`overrides` entry scoped to that package only. Do not reach for `--legacy-peer-deps` or downgrade the project's TypeScript version.
18	
19	## LRN-2026-08-21-c2: openapi-typescript still pins peer typescript ^5.x, so Angular 22 rejects it
20	
21	```meta
22	date: 2026-08-21
23	project: arcade
24	stack: [angular, typescript, openapi]
25	req: []
26	auditor_run: scaffold@p4
27	severity: major
28	origin: human
29	```
30	
31	**What happened.** `npm install -D openapi-typescript@7.13.0` failed with ERESOLVE against a fresh Angular 22 app. Angular 22 ships TypeScript 6.0; openapi-typescript's latest release and its `next` tag both declare `peerDependencies.typescript: "^5.x"`.
32	
33	**Why it matters.** The reflex fixes both cost something. `--legacy-peer-deps` or an `overrides` block silences the check but leaves a false constraint in the lockfile that the next person has to re-litigate. Downgrading TypeScript to satisfy a codegen tool is backwards: the tool never type-checks the project, it only emits a `.d.ts`.
34	
35	**Pattern to encode.** When a code-generation CLI conflicts on peers with the framework's TypeScript, do not install it. 270	## LRN-2026-08-24-c: A client-asserted identity is a claim, not a proof -- cryptographic verification is required the moment an action is account-scoped and irreversible
271	
272	```meta
273	date: 2026-08-24
274	project: arcade-web
275	stack: [angular, amplify-gen2, dynamodb, cognito, lambda-function-url]
276	req: [REQ-ARC-14]
277	auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
278	severity: HIGH
279	origin: crew-auditor
280	```
281	
282	**What happened:** REQ-ARC-14's scout contract recommended trusting a body-passed `sub`, "verified" only by confirming the caller held some valid signed credential -- the SAME trust model this codebase's other platform functions already use for their client-asserted `identityId`. An operator ruling overrode this as forgeable: any signed caller (even a guest's own valid credentials) could assert another account's `sub` in the body and permanently steal a resource tied to it. The fix cryptographically verifies the caller's Cognito ID token against the pool's JWKS and acts only on the token's own verified claim. The auditor independently re-attacked the deployed endpoint: forged/tampered/missing tokens all rejected at 401; a forged `sub` riding alongside a real token was structurally unreachable (the handler never parses it); and a real token submitted while a *different* identity's credentials did the IAM signing still resolved to the token's own account, never the signer's -- proving the two trust layers (coarse IAM signing, fine-grained token verification) are genuinely independent and composable, not redundant.
283	
284	**Why it matters:** most authenticated actions in a system are fine with "some valid signed caller" as the whole trust model -- a guest's own pairing, moves, and presence are self-contained to that one session and cost nothing if merely coarse-grained. The trust model silently stops being sufficient the instant an action's correctness depends on WHICH specific account is calling AND its effect is durable/hard-to-reverse (here: permanent, exclusive ownership). Reusing the codebase's existing, working trust pattern by default is the natural move and was exactly the wrong one here.

72	export function applyMove(state: GameState, move: Move): MoveOutcome;
73	// Pure. Never mutates `state` or `move`. Returns a new GameState on success.
74	// On rejection returns { ok: false, reason } and NO state. The caller keeps its stored state.
75	
76	export function readAuthoritativeState(state: GameState): GameState;
77	// Pure. Returns a deep-frozen copy of board, turn, participants, and result.
78	// Mutating the returned value must not change `state`.
79	```
80	
81	### State invariants
82	
83	- `turn` is `null` if and only if `result` is non-null.
84	- A win sets `result = { outcome: 'win', winner, winnerId, line }`, where `winnerId = participants[winner]` and `line` is the matching `WINNING_LINES` entry.
85	- A draw sets `result = { outcome: 'draw' }`. This happens only when the board is full and `findWinningLine` returns null.
86	- A move that completes a line on the 9th cell is a win, not a draw. The win check runs before the draw check.
87	
88	### applyMove check order (first failure wins)
89	
90	1. `not_a_participant`: `move.playerId` matches neither `participants.X` nor `participants.O`. This runs first so outsiders learn nothing about the game's status.
91	2. `game_finished`: `result !== null`.
92	3. `not_your_turn`: `participants[turn] !== move.playerId`.
93	4. `invalid_cell`: `!Number.isInteger(cell) || cell < 0 || cell > 8`.
94	5. `cell_occupied`: `board[cell] !== null`.
95	
96	On success: place the mark, then `findWinningLine`. If a line exists, set the win result and `turn = null`. Otherwise, if no `null` cell remains, set the draw result and `turn = null`. Otherwise flip `turn`.

3	
4	## LRN-2026-08-24-c: A client-asserted identity is a claim, not a proof -- cryptographic verification is required the moment an action is account-scoped and irreversible
5	
6	```meta
7	date: 2026-08-24
8	project: arcade-web
9	stack: [angular, amplify-gen2, dynamodb, cognito, lambda-function-url]
10	req: [REQ-ARC-14]
11	auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-24
12	severity: HIGH
13	origin: crew-auditor
14	```
15	
16	**What happened:** REQ-ARC-14's scout contract recommended trusting a body-passed `sub`, "verified" only by confirming the caller held some valid signed credential -- the SAME trust model this codebase's other platform functions already use for their client-asserted `identityId`. An operator ruling overrode this as forgeable: any signed caller (even a guest's own valid credentials) could assert another account's `sub` in the body and permanently steal a resource tied to it. The fix cryptographically verifies the caller's Cognito ID token against the pool's JWKS and acts only on the token's own verified claim. The auditor independently re-attacked the deployed endpoint: forged/tampered/missing tokens all rejected at 401; a forged `sub` riding alongside a real token was structurally unreachable (the handler never parses it); and a real token submitted while a *different* identity's credentials did the IAM signing still resolved to the token's own account, never the signer's -- proving the two trust layers (coarse IAM signing, fine-grained token verification) are genuinely independent and composable, not redundant.
17	
18	**Why it matters:** most authenticated actions in a system are fine with "some valid signed caller" as the whole trust model -- a guest's own pairing, moves, and presence are self-contained to that one session and cost nothing if merely coarse-grained. The trust model silently stops being sufficient the instant an action's correctness depends on WHICH specific account is calling AND its effect is durable/hard-to-reverse (here: permanent, exclusive ownership). Reusing the codebase's existing, working trust pattern by default is the natural move and was exactly the wrong one here.
19	
20	**Pattern to encode:** before trusting any client-asserted identity field (a body `sub`, a JWT claim read without signature verification, a session id used as if it were proof), ask: does this action's correctness depend on WHICH identity is calling (not just "some" valid one), and is the effect account-scoped and durable/irreversible? If yes to both, the identity must be cryptographically verified server-side against its own issuer (JWKS/JWT verification, not "the caller holds a valid credential for some other coarser-grained gate"), and the verified claim -- never a request-body field of the same name -- is the only thing the handler may act on.
21	
22	## LRN-2026-08-22-a: 100% coverage does not prove a signal-exposed WS message type is actually consumed by the UI
23	
24	```meta
25	date: 2026-08-22
26	project: arcade-web
27	stack: [angular, vitest, websocket, signals]
28	req: [REQ-ARC-7]
29	auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-22
30	severity: blocker
31	```
32	
33	**What happened.** `GameSocketService` (the coder-spec's mandated single owning service for `/ws/game`) correctly exposed all seven server-to-client message types as readonly signals, including `moveError`. The tester wrote a passing unit test asserting `moveError()` updates when a `move_error` frame arrives. Coverage reported 100% line/branch/function on the service and on every component. But no component ever read `gameSocket.moveError()` -- the handoff contract's documented UI action ("transient rejection cue: shake the cell, toast the message; route non-recoverable codes to an error state") was never built. The auditor found this only by grepping for the signal's call sites outside test files, not from any tool output.
34	
35	**Why it matters.** Coverage tools measure whether producer-side code executed, not whether a consumer exists downstream. A well-tested, fully-covered signal or observable can be entirely dead from the user's perspective while every quality gate reports green. This is structurally invisible to line/branch coverage because there is no untaken branch -- the producer code runs fine every time.
36	
37	**Pattern to encode.** When a spec mandates a service expose "every message type as a signal" (fan-out architecture), the audit checklist must separately verify each exposed signal has at least one non-test call site, not just that the producer path is covered. Grep for `<signalName>(` outside `*.spec.ts` as a cheap first pass before trusting coverage numbers on message-routing services.
38	
39	## LRN-2026-08-22-i: Exhaustive per-value test coverage belongs at the layer that branches on the value, not the layer that merely passes it through
40	
41	```meta
42	date: 2026-08-22
43	project: arcade-web
44	stack: [angular, vitest, websocket]
45	req: [REQ-ARC-7]
46	auditor_run: frontend/AUDIT_REPORT.md@2026-08-22
47	severity: suggestion
48	```
49	
50	**What happened.** A prior audit suggested a service-layer WS-message spec should parameterize over all 7 members of a discriminated-union code field, since it only tested 2 directly. A later fix exhaustively covered all 7 at the consumer layer (the component that maps each code to distinct UI text) instead. Re-examining the service's actual routing code showed it performs zero per-code branching -- it stores the whole message object regardless of which of the 7 values arrived. Parameterizing the service spec over all 7 values would have tested nothing the 2-value spec did not already prove; the router doesn't care which value it is.
51	
52	**Why it matters.** "Only N of M enum values are tested at this layer" is not automatically a gap. Whether it is a gap depends on whether that layer's code varies its behavior by value. Flagging it reflexively, without checking for branching, sends fix effort to the wrong file and can produce redundant tests that inflate a suite without adding assurance.
53	
54	**Pattern to encode.** Before treating partial per-value coverage as a finding, check whether the flagged code path branches on the value at all. If it's a pure pass-through, the exhaustive check belongs at the nearest layer that actually discriminates.

61	## Architecture Patterns

63	### Standalone components only
64	No `NgModule`. New code uses `standalone: true` (the default in Angular 21+). Components, directives, and pipes import their own dependencies via the `imports` array.

66	### Signals for reactive state
67	- Component state: `signal()`, `computed()`, `linkedSignal()`.
68	- Async: `resource()` / `httpResource()` (Angular 20+). Falls back to `toSignal(observable$)` when interop with RxJS is required.
69	- Forms: signal-based forms (`Control` from `@angular/forms/signals`) for new code; existing reactive forms (`FormGroup`) are tolerated but new feature work uses signals.
70	- Do NOT use `BehaviorSubject` for component-local state. Use `signal()`.
71	
72	### OnPush change detection
73	Every new component declares `changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`. The default `Default` strategy is forbidden in new code; it costs performance and hides re-render bugs.
74	
75	### Dependency injection
76	- `inject()` function inside the constructor body or as a class field. Constructor parameter injection is the older style; new code uses `inject()`.
77	- `providedIn: 'root'` for app-wide services. Feature-scoped services use a feature-local provider.

53	### Module decisions (proposed names; the coder spec has no naming rules for this module)
54	
55	- File: `amplify/shared/game-rules.ts`. One file. The Lambdas import it later. Signatures below are binding for the coder.
56	- Board index: `0..8`, row-major (`index = row * 3 + col`). Win lines are the 8 triples of indices.
57	- Marks: `'X'` moves first. Seats are `participants.X` and `participants.O`.
58	- Player identity: `PlayerId` is a plain string compared with `===`. The module trusts the id it receives. The server layer must derive it from a verified identity (see Handoff Notes).

60	### Function contract
61	
62	```ts
63	export const WINNING_LINES: readonly WinningLine[];   // exactly 8 entries: 3 rows, 3 cols, 2 diagonals
64	
65	export function createGame(participants: { readonly X: PlayerId; readonly O: PlayerId }): GameState;
66	// Empty board, turn 'X', result null. Recommended: throw RangeError when either id is '' or X === O.
67	// Not an AC, so at most one test if implemented.
68	
69	export function findWinningLine(board: Board): { readonly mark: Mark; readonly line: WinningLine } | null;
70	// Scans WINNING_LINES in array order; returns the first all-same non-null line, else null.
71	
72	export function applyMove(state: GameState, move: Move): MoveOutcome;
73	// Pure. Never mutates `state` or `move`. Returns a new GameState on success.
74	// On rejection returns { ok: false, reason } and NO state. The caller keeps its stored state.
75	
76	export function readAuthoritativeState(state: GameState): GameState;
77	// Pure. Returns a deep-frozen copy of board, turn, participants, and result.
78	// Mutating the returned value must not change `state`.
79	```
80	
81	### State invariants
82	
83	- `turn` is `null` if and only if `result` is non-null.
84	- A win sets `result = { outcome: 'win', winner, winnerId, line }`, where `winnerId = participants[winner]` and `line` is the matching `WINNING_LINES` entry.
85	- A draw sets `result = { outcome: 'draw' }`. This happens only when the board is full and `findWinningLine` returns null.
86	- A move that completes a line on the 9th cell is a win, not a draw. The win check runs before the draw check.
87	
88	### applyMove check order (first failure wins)
89	
90	1. `not_a_participant`: `move.playerId` matches neither `participants.X` nor `participants.O`. This runs first so outsiders learn nothing about the game's status.
91	2. `game_finished`: `result !== null`.
92	3. `not_your_turn`: `participants[turn] !== move.playerId`.
93	4. `invalid_cell`: `!Number.isInteger(cell) || cell < 0 || cell > 8`.
94	5. `cell_occupied`: `board[cell] !== null`.
95	
96	On success: place the mark, then `findWinningLine`. If a line exists, set the win result and `turn = null`. Otherwise, if no `null` cell remains, set the draw result and `turn = null`. Otherwise flip `turn`.
